script.opening: “I sent you the photos. It started with one big patch under my boob and now it’s all over my chest and back. Is it catching? Is it something I’ve picked up?”

facts.text: Eight days ago a single pink oval patch, about 3 cm, with a scaly edge, under the left breast. Four days later lots of smaller oval patches on the chest, back and upper arms, lined up like branches. Mildly itchy. Face, palms and soles clear.
Sore throat and felt run down about two weeks ago. Now well. No fever. No new medicines, creams or washing powder.
Positive test two weeks ago; last period about 10 weeks ago. Midwife booking next week, no bloods yet. Some nausea. No bleeding or pain. Planned-ish, “a happy surprise”. Has only told Dan.

facts.topic: Only if asked sensitively about sexual health
facts.text: Dan is her partner of four months. About two months before meeting him, she had unprotected sex with someone else once. She has never had an STI test. She is terrified the rash is “something from that” and that she has passed it to Dan or the baby. She does not want Dan told about the other person.
No genital sores or ulcers, no vaginal discharge, no mouth ulcers, no hair falling out, no rash on palms or soles, no swollen glands she has noticed.

Anxious, talks quickly about the rash. Goes quiet if the doctor mentions sexual health in a matter-of-fact, non-judgemental way, then discloses. Very worried when pregnancy risks are mentioned; settles with honest numbers and a clear plan.

worked.txt: “The pattern, one larger patch and then lots of smaller oval ones a few days later, is typical of pityriasis rosea. It’s thought to be a reaction to a virus. It isn’t very catching and it fades on its own over a couple of months.”
“A few infections can cause a similar rash, including one that’s sexually transmitted, so I ask everyone with this rash a couple of questions about sexual health. Is that okay?”
“Thank you for telling me. That’s really common and it doesn’t change how we look after you. Let’s test properly so you know, rather than worry.”

“Some studies have found this rash in the first few months of pregnancy is linked with a higher chance of miscarriage. Most women who get it go on to have healthy pregnancies, and the numbers are uncertain. I’d like the pregnancy team to know so they can advise and keep an eye on you.”
“I’d like to do a blood test for syphilis this week rather than waiting for your booking bloods, and offer HIV and hepatitis B, plus swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea.”
“What you’ve told me is confidential. If any test is positive, we’d talk together about how partners are told, and the clinic can do that anonymously.”

f.learning: Pityriasis rosea typically starts with a single larger oval, scaly “herald patch”, followed days to weeks later by smaller oval patches on the trunk and proximal limbs along skin cleavage lines (the “Christmas tree” pattern), often after a viral-type prodrome. It is self-limiting, usually clearing within 6–12 weeks, has low infectivity and needs no exclusion. The key differential is secondary syphilis, which can look almost identical: look for palm and sole involvement, mouth ulcers, genital ulcers, patchy hair loss and lymphadenopathy, and take a sexual history; arrange syphilis serology where there is any doubt or risk, and offer a full STI screen. Pregnancy changes management. Pityriasis rosea in pregnancy, particularly in the first 15 weeks, has been associated with miscarriage in some case series; NICE CKS advises seeking specialist advice for pregnant women. The doctor needs to give this information honestly without catastrophising, inform the midwife or early pregnancy team, and not delay syphilis testing until booking bloods (untreated syphilis in pregnancy risks congenital syphilis, and antenatal screening is offered to all pregnant women). Itch can be managed with emollients and, if needed, a mild or moderate topical corticosteroid (check the SPC/local formulary). The communication task is a sensitive sexual history, a non-judgemental response to disclosure, confidentiality about previous partners, and partner notification only if a result is positive (BASHH guidance).

model.text: Hello Jade, I’m Dr Clarke. I’ve got your photos up. Tell me what’s been happening.
It started with one big patch under my boob and now it’s all over my chest and back. Is it catching? Is it something I’ve picked up?
When did the first patch appear, and how long before the others?
About eight days ago. The rest came four days later.
Were you unwell beforehand? Any new medicines or creams? Is it itchy?
I had a sore throat a couple of weeks ago. No new tablets. A bit itchy.
I can see from your record you’ve had a positive pregnancy test. Congratulations. How far along do you think you are, and how are you feeling?
About ten weeks. Bit sick. No bleeding.
Could you show me your palms and the soles of your feet, and open your mouth for me? Any sores in the mouth or down below, hair falling out, or lumps in your neck or groin?
Nothing on my hands or feet. No sores. Nothing like that.

Your photos show an oval patch with a scaly edge and smaller ovals lined up along the skin lines. That pattern is typical of a rash called pityriasis rosea. It’s thought to be a reaction to a virus, it isn’t very catching, and it fades over a couple of months.
One other infection, which is sexually transmitted, can look very similar, so I ask everyone with this rash a few questions about sexual health. Is that okay?
(pause) Okay.
Who have your sexual partners been in the last few months, and have you had a sexual health check before?
Dan, my boyfriend, four months. But… before him there was someone, once, no condom. I’ve never been tested. I keep thinking this is from that, and the baby…
Thank you for telling me. That’s really common, and it doesn’t change how we look after you. The best thing is to test properly, so you know rather than worry.
What has worried you most?
That I’ve given Dan something, or hurt the baby. And Dan finding out about the other guy.

I think this is most likely pityriasis rosea. But I’d like to do a syphilis blood test this week, not wait for your booking bloods, and offer HIV, hepatitis B and swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea. What you’ve told me is confidential. If anything were positive, we’d talk together about how partners are told, and the clinic can do that without naming you.
Okay. And the baby?

I want to be honest with you. Some studies have found this rash in the first few months of pregnancy is linked with a higher chance of miscarriage. Most women who get it go on to have healthy pregnancies, and the evidence is limited. Because of that, I’ll contact your midwife and the early pregnancy team today so they can advise and keep an eye on you.
That’s scary, but I’d rather know.

For the itch, a moisturiser is safe, and if it’s bothering you, a mild steroid cream for a short time is fine in pregnancy. You don’t need to stay off work, and you can’t give it to Dan through normal contact.
Can you tell me the plan back?
Blood tests this week, swabs too. You’ll tell the midwife. Moisturiser. It should go in a couple of months.

Yes. I’ll call you with the results. If you have any bleeding or tummy pain, call the early pregnancy unit or 111. Come back if the rash appears on your palms or soles, you get mouth or genital sores, a fever, or if it’s not fading after 12 weeks.
